title: MATH GAOKAO - 415
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Verify that each term in a kinematic equation has the same physical dimension.
questions.question: In the equation \(s=v_0t+\frac{1}{2}at^2\), which statement about the dimensions of the two terms on the right-hand side is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both \(v_0t\) and \(\frac{1}{2}at^2\) have the dimension of length.

options.label: B
options.text: Only \(v_0t\) has the dimension of length.

questions.explanation: The dimension of \(v_0t\) is \((\frac{L}{T})\cdot T=L\). The dimension of \(\frac{1}{2}at^2\) is \((\frac{L}{T^2})\cdot T^2=L\). Therefore both terms have the dimension of length, which is consistent with the left-hand side \(s\).
questions.hint: Recall that velocity has dimension \(\frac{L}{T}\) and acceleration has dimension \(\frac{L}{T^2}\).

questions.learningObjective: Convert a speed from kilometers per hour to meters per second.
questions.question: A car travels at \(72\text{ km/h}\). What is this speed in meters per second?
questions.explanation:
Convert kilometers to meters and hours to seconds:
\[
\begin{aligned}
72\text{ km/h}&=72\cdot\frac{1000\text{ m}}{3600\text{ s}} \\
&=72\cdot\frac{5}{18}\text{ m/s} \\
&=20\text{ m/s}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the speed is \(20\text{ m/s}\).
questions.hint: Multiply by \(1000\) to convert kilometers to meters and divide by \(3600\) to convert hours to seconds.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which formula is dimensionally consistent with the definition of force.
questions.question: Which equation is dimensionally consistent? Here \(F\) is force, \(m\) is mass, \(v\) is speed, and \(a\) is acceleration.
questions.explanation: Force has dimension \(MLT^{-2}\). For \(F=ma\), the right-hand side has dimension \(M\cdot LT^{-2}=MLT^{-2}\), so it is consistent. For \(F=mv\), the right-hand side has dimension \(M\cdot LT^{-1}=MLT^{-1}\), which is not the dimension of force.
questions.hint: Compare the dimensions of force, mass, velocity, and acceleration.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the SI unit of a constant in a quadratic distance model.
questions.question: A model gives distance \(d\) in meters as \(d=kt^2\), where \(t\) is in seconds. What is the SI unit of \(k\)?
questions.explanation:
Since \(d=kt^2\), we have \(k=\frac{d}{t^2}\). The unit of \(d\) is meters and the unit of \(t^2\) is seconds squared, so the unit of \(k\) is
\[
\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}.
\]
questions.hint: Rearrange the equation as \(k=\frac{d}{t^2}\) and divide the units.

questions.concept: Dimensional Analysis of a Pendulum Formula
questions.learningObjective: Determine the SI unit of an expression inside a pendulum period formula.
questions.question: For a simple pendulum, \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\). If \(L\) is in meters and \(g\) is in meters per second squared, what is the SI unit of \(\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\)?
questions.explanation:
The units of \(\frac{L}{g}\) are
\[
\frac{\text{m}}{\text{m/s}^2}=\text{s}^2.
\]
Taking the square root gives \(\text{s}\). Therefore \(\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\) has the SI unit second, consistent with a period.
questions.hint: Simplify the units inside the square root before taking the square root.

questions.concept: Units of Volume in a Geometric Model
questions.learningObjective: Determine the unit of volume when the radius is measured in centimeters.
questions.question: The volume of a sphere is \(V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\). If the radius \(r\) is measured in centimeters, what is the unit of \(V\)?
questions.explanation: Since \(r\) has unit \(\text{cm}\), the expression \(r^3\) has unit \(\text{cm}^3\). The constants \(\frac{4}{3}\) and \(\pi\) are dimensionless, so \(V\) also has unit \(\text{cm}^3\).
questions.hint: Cubing a length unit produces a volume unit.

questions.learningObjective: Use a length scale ratio to find a model length.
questions.question: A scale model of a car uses a length scale of \(1:20\). If the real car is \(4\text{ m}\) long, how long is the model?
questions.explanation:
The model length is
\[
4\text{ m}\div 20=0.2\text{ m}.
\]
Converting to centimeters,
\[
0.2\text{ m}=20\text{ cm}.
\]
questions.hint: Divide the real length by the scale factor, then convert meters to centimeters.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which expression has the dimension of acceleration.
questions.question: Which expression has the dimension of acceleration? Here \(v\) is speed and \(r\) is a length.
questions.explanation:
Velocity \(v\) has dimension \(\frac{L}{T}\), and radius \(r\) has dimension \(L\). Then
\[
\frac{v^2}{r}\text{ has dimension }\frac{(\frac{L}{T})^2}{L}=\frac{L}{T^2},
\]
which is acceleration. In contrast,
\[
\frac{v}{r}\text{ has dimension }\frac{\frac{L}{T}}{L}=\frac{1}{T},
\]
which is not acceleration.
questions.hint: Write velocity as length per time and radius as length.

questions.learningObjective: Check which pressure formula is dimensionally consistent.
questions.question: Let \(P\) be pressure (force per unit area), \(\rho\) be mass density, \(g\) be gravitational acceleration, and \(h\) be a height. Which proposed equation is dimensionally consistent?
questions.explanation:
Density has dimension \(\frac{M}{L^3}\), gravitational acceleration has dimension \(\frac{L}{T^2}\), and height has dimension \(L\). Thus
\[
\rho gh\text{ has dimension }\frac{M}{L^3}\cdot\frac{L}{T^2}\cdot L=\frac{M}{LT^2},
\]
which is pressure. For \(\rho gh^2\), the dimension would be
\[
\frac{M}{L^3}\cdot\frac{L}{T^2}\cdot L^2=\frac{M}{T^2},
\]
which is not pressure.
questions.hint: Use the dimensions of density, gravitational acceleration, and height.

questions.learningObjective: Determine how volume changes under a length scale factor.
questions.question: A solid model is scaled down so that every length is \(\frac{1}{10}\) of the real object. If the real volume is \(1000\text{ cm}^3\), what is the model volume?
questions.explanation:
For similar solids, volume scales as the cube of the length scale factor. The length scale factor is \(\frac{1}{10}\), so the volume scale factor is
\[
\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^3=\frac{1}{1000}.
\]
Therefore the model volume is
\[
1000\cdot\frac{1}{1000}=1\text{ cm}^3.
\]
questions.hint: Determine how volume scaling depends on the length scale factor.
